title: Not quite eye to A.I.: student and teacher perspectives on the use of generative artificial intelligence in the writing process
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students and teachers view the acceptable use of generative artificial intelligence in the writing process, motivated by the rapid spread of tools such as ChatGPT and concerns about plagiarism, academic integrity, authorship, and appropriate classroom use. The study asks how undergraduate students and teachers judge different uses of GenAI across multiple writing tasks and whether their views differ. It is framed as an effort to inform evidence-based institutional guidelines and teacher professional development rather than to test learning effects.

The authors used a cross-sectional questionnaire survey. Participants reviewed example ChatGPT prompts and outputs for six writing-related tasks: brainstorming, outlining, writing, revising, teacher feedback, and teacher evaluation. For each task, respondents rated the appropriateness of four forms of use: using AI when already competent at the task, using AI output as a model or idea source, submitting AI-generated output with disclosure, and submitting AI-generated output without disclosure. The study also included survey items on perceived usefulness of AI, concern about AI use, openness to technology, familiarity with AI, and institutional policy/training.

The sample included 226 participants: 158 students and 68 teachers. Students were primarily undergraduates at a public research university in the United States, with a small number of graduate students. Teachers were recruited from multiple institutions worldwide, primarily adult/university-level language educators, with a very small number of K-12 teachers. Thus, the context is predominantly higher education, especially writing and language teaching, rather than direct K-12 literacy instruction.

The main conclusion is that students and teachers broadly agree that GenAI is more acceptable when used for support purposes, such as brainstorming, outlining, generating models, or offloading tasks the user already knows how to do, and less acceptable when used to complete assignments for submission, especially without disclosure. Both groups viewed undisclosed use as the least acceptable practice. The paper also concludes that institutions and classrooms were largely unprepared for GenAI: most respondents reported little or no AI-related training, and many reported lacking clear policy guidance. The authors argue for explicit institutional guidelines, transparency about AI use, and teacher professional development to support ethical and educationally appropriate integration of generative AI.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed cross-sectional survey study with clear methods, sample sizes, and statistical comparisons, but it is non-random, perception-based, and not designed to estimate causal learning effects. It provides one credibility criterion (transparent empirical methodology) but lacks experimental or quasi-experimental design.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows meaningful but perception-based signals about institutional readiness and acceptable use boundaries rather than direct measured learning impacts. Effects on practice are plausible but unclear in magnitude, with no standardized achievement effect sizes reported.

interventions.use_case: Survey-based evaluation of ChatGPT/GenAI use across stages of the writing process (brainstorming, outlining, drafting, revising, teacher feedback, and evaluation) by students and teachers.
Teacher-facing use of ChatGPT as an automated writing feedback and evaluation tool for commenting on student paragraphs.
GenAI used as a writing assistant for idea generation, outlining, drafting, and revision in academic writing contexts.

finding.finding_summary: In this survey of university students (n=158) and teachers (n=68), respondents generally viewed GenAI as acceptable for literacy-process support such as brainstorming, outlining models, and revision models, but unacceptable for submitting AI-produced writing as one's own. For example, both groups were mostly accepting of using GenAI as a model for brainstorming and writing, while teachers were significantly less accepting than students of submitting GenAI-written or revised text with or without disclosure (multiple Mann-Whitney tests reported, e.g., writing with disclosure U=4311.5, p=0.011; writing without disclosure U=4245.5, p<0.001); no standardized effect sizes were reported, only small r values for group differences.
finding.measure: Perceived appropriateness of GenAI use in the writing process across brainstorming, outlining, writing, and revising tasks on 5-point Likert survey items
finding.std_deviation: reported for task means; e.g., writing division B student SD=1.42, teacher SD=1.30

finding.finding_summary: Respondents perceived AI as potentially useful for both students and teachers, suggesting possible efficiency benefits, especially for teacher feedback and evaluation support. Teachers were significantly more likely than students to agree that AI would be useful for teachers (mean 3.99 vs. 3.32 on a 5-point scale; U=7098, p<0.001), and both groups were generally accepting of teacher use of GenAI as a model for feedback/evaluation rather than undisclosed replacement of teacher judgment.
finding.measure: Survey items on perceived utility of AI for students/teachers and acceptability of AI-supported feedback/evaluation
finding.std_deviation: reported for utility items; e.g., AI useful for teachers student SD=1.18, teacher SD=0.74

finding.finding_summary: The study found substantial institutional unpreparedness for GenAI governance and training. Only 5.9% of teachers reported their institution had an AI policy, 4.4% reported receiving AI training, and 10.3% reported educating students about appropriate AI use; student reports from a single university were also mixed on whether any policy existed, indicating limited institutional readiness despite widespread concern about AI use.
finding.measure: Yes/no survey items on institutional AI policy, training, and teacher preparation regarding appropriate AI use
finding.study_size: n=226 overall; teacher policy/training items n=68, student policy/training items n=158

finding.finding_summary: Perceptions in the study imply respondents distinguish between acceptable AI use that may scaffold idea generation and organization versus unacceptable use that may replace core authorship and thinking work. Participants were generally supportive of AI for generating ideas/models but opposed undisclosed AI completion of writing tasks, reflecting concern that overreliance could undermine writing-related critical thinking and ownership; however, no direct performance measure of durable skills was collected.
finding.measure: Perceived appropriateness of AI for ideation/modeling versus completing writing tasks
finding.std_deviation: reported across Likert means, exact durable-skill SD not separately reported
